passage:
Tuesday: Pranav dropped the easy catch that lost the inter-class match. While the others cheered the winners, he hid behind the equipment shed with his face on his knees. "I'm so stupid. I'm useless," he muttered when Chandrika Ma'am found him. She sat on an upturned bucket nearby. "You dropped one catch. That's something that happened, not who you are. You're safe here. Take your time."
Thursday: Pranav came to practice but stood at the very back. Ma'am threw him easy catches, one after another, and said only, "Watch the ball into your hands."
The following Monday: A high ball came his way in the lunchtime game. Pranav caught it, looked round for Ma'am, and grinned.

qa.q: Where did Pranav hide after the match?
qa.a: Behind the equipment shed.

qa.q: What was Pranav feeling when he muttered that he was stupid?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and humiliated, turning one dropped catch into a judgement about his whole self.

qa.q: What helped Pranav return to the game?
qa.a: Ma'am's words separating the catch from who he is, then quiet practice with easy catches and one simple tip, without raking up the loss.

qa.q: How might Chandrika Ma'am have seen Pranav behind the shed?
qa.a: She likely saw a child who needed safety more than a lesson, so she sat nearby instead of lecturing.

grounding: It illustrates a child hiding and calling himself stupid after a failure, and an adult separating the act from the person and offering safety.

passage: I'm Ankita, and this happened in the summer holidays. My cousin Jaya had a new set of sketch pens that nobody was allowed to touch. When Jaya went to the market with Chachi, I used them anyway for my poster, and I left the lid off the purple one. When they came back, I couldn't look at Jaya. I started talking very fast about the weather and the poster competition and how purple is a boring colour anyway. Then Jaya found the dried-up pen. My stomach dropped and I said, "It was me. I'm sorry." Chachi didn't shout. She said, "Thank you for telling the truth. What can you do to fix it?" I gave Jaya my own purple crayon and helped finish Jaya's card. We were fine by evening.

qa.q: What colour was the pen that dried up?
qa.a: Purple.

qa.q: Why did Ankita talk so fast about the weather and the poster competition?
qa.a: Ankita felt guilty and nervous, and over-explaining was a way to avoid Jaya's eyes and the dried pen.

qa.q: What kept Ankita's guilt in proportion and useful?
qa.a: Chachi thanked Ankita for the truth and asked about fixing it instead of shouting, which turned guilt into repair.

qa.q: How might Jaya have felt on finding the dried pen?
qa.a: Jaya was likely annoyed and let down that the new set had been used, though the quick confession and help eased it by evening.

grounding: It shows a child who broke a rule avoiding eye contact, over-explaining and then confessing, with an adult keeping the guilt proportionate and focused on repair.

passage: The temple fair in Malpur glowed with bulbs as the sun went down. Yusuf tugged at Swati Aunty's dupatta, eyes huge. "Please, please, just one more ride on the giant wheel. Pleeease." His voice went soft and small. Swati Aunty, who had brought him along with her own children, crouched down. "You really love that wheel, don't you? From the top you can see the whole village." Yusuf nodded hard. "But your Ammi said home before dark, and the last bus leaves soon. We keep our promise." Yusuf's lip trembled. She squeezed his hand. "Next fair day, we ride the wheel first, before anything else." On the bus, Yusuf pressed his face to the window, watching the wheel's lights grow smaller.

qa.q: What did Yusuf want one more ride on?
qa.a: The giant wheel.

qa.q: What did Yusuf's trembling lip suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and sad about leaving, having hoped his pleading would change the answer.

qa.q: How did Swati Aunty hear Yusuf's need while keeping the limit?
qa.a: She named how much he loved the wheel, gave the reason for leaving, and offered a clear plan to ride it first next time.

qa.q: How might Swati Aunty have felt holding the limit?
qa.a: She likely felt fond of Yusuf and a little sorry for him, but responsible for the promise to his Ammi and the last bus.

grounding: It illustrates a child pleading with big eyes and a soft voice, and an adult hearing the wish while holding a fair limit.

passage: Mridul's skate caught a crack in the colony road and he went down hard, palms first. Ira skidded to a stop and knelt beside him. His hands were scraped and his eyes were full. Ira nearly said, "It's nothing, get up," but she saw his chin shaking. Instead she patted his shoulder. "That was a big fall. I'm staying right here." Mridul sniffed. "Mummy will be so angry. I broke the rule about the main road." Ira wanted to say, "She won't be," but she didn't know that. "I'll come with you when you tell her," she said. They walked home slowly, Ira carrying both pairs of skates. Mridul's mummy washed his palms first and talked about the rule afterwards.

qa.q: What did Mridul's skate catch?
qa.a: A crack in the colony road.

qa.q: Why did Ira hold back from saying "She won't be"?
qa.a: Ira felt caring but wanted to stay honest, and didn't want to make an empty promise about something she couldn't know.

qa.q: Which of Ira's words matched what Mridul needed?
qa.a: Naming the big fall, staying close, and offering to come along when he told Mummy, instead of 'it's nothing' or a promise she couldn't keep 🙂

qa.q: What was the fall like for Mridul?
qa.a: Painful and scary, with scraped palms and a shaking chin, plus worry that Mummy would be angry about the rule.

grounding: It shows a child reassuring a friend after a fall by staying close and matching words to the friend's need, while avoiding an empty promise.

passage: Jatin, you nodded at everything I said about fractions and then got all three sums wrong? Sit, let me tell you about my first year of teaching. I was Madhuri Miss then, twenty-two and very sure of myself. There was a boy called Kiran, eight years old, who nodded at every instruction. Yes, Miss. Yes, Miss. But his copy was full of wrong answers, and he fidgeted and stared at the blackboard as if it were a wall. I thought he wasn't trying. One day I asked him, "Tell me in your own words what I just said." He went red and whispered, "I don't know what 'remainder' means." All those nods, and he had been hiding it. After that, I asked every child to explain back. So, Jatin: tell me in your words what a fraction is.

qa.q: Which word did Kiran not understand?
qa.a: 'Remainder'.

qa.q: Why did Kiran keep nodding when he didn't understand?
qa.a: He likely felt embarrassed and afraid of looking foolish, so he hid his confusion behind 'Yes, Miss'.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Madhuri Miss taught?
qa.a: Asking Kiran to explain in his own words showed the missing word, so she began asking every child to explain back.

qa.q: How did young Madhuri Miss see Kiran at first?
qa.a: She thought he wasn't trying, reading his wrong answers and fidgeting as carelessness rather than confusion.

grounding: It illustrates a child hiding confusion behind nods and wrong answers, and asking the child to explain back as the way to check understanding.

passage: I'm Pooja, Tushar's big sister, and I was at the bus stop when it happened. Hrithik announced that swallowed gum stays in your stomach for seven years. The other kids gasped. Tushar tilted his head. "Really? How do you know?" "My cousin said so. Everyone knows." Tushar frowned, the way he does at a hard sum. That evening he asked me to help him look it up in the big science book at home, and the next morning he asked his science teacher. Both said gum does not stay for years. At the bus stop, Tushar told Hrithik calmly, not showing off. Hrithik said, "Okay, but my cousin also says sharks can smell one drop of blood from miles away." Tushar laughed. "Let's check that one too."

qa.q: How long did Hrithik say swallowed gum stays in your stomach?
qa.a: Seven years.

qa.q: What might Tushar's frown suggest?
qa.a: He seemed doubtful and curious, turning the claim over like a hard sum, though Pooja can only guess from his face.

qa.q: What made Tushar's doubt healthy rather than rude?
qa.a: He asked for the source, checked two good sources, accepted what they said, and shared it calmly without showing off.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when Tushar corrected him?
qa.a: Hrithik may have felt a little embarrassed, but because Tushar was calm, he stayed friendly and even offered another claim to check.

grounding: It shows a child answering an odd claim with 'Really? How do you know?', checking sources and accepting good evidence, as seen by an older sibling.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 5, maths hour
Today I asked the class how many different ways we could make 10 using only odd numbers. Avni's hand shot up at once. Harsha went quiet, looked out of the window and tapped a pencil against his chin. In the past I would have moved on, thinking Harsha was lost. This time I said, "Let's give everyone ten more seconds." I counted in my head. At about eight, Harsha turned back and said, "You can never do it with three odd numbers, because three odd numbers always make an odd number." That was exactly the idea I had hoped someone would find. Next step: I will keep a waiting pause after every big question, and tell the class why.

qa.q: What maths question did the teacher ask?
qa.a: How many different ways they could make 10 using only odd numbers.

qa.q: What might Harsha have been feeling and thinking while he looked out of the window?
qa.a: He was thinking hard and curious about a pattern, not lost or bored, as his answer showed.

qa.q: What did the teacher change, and why did it help?
qa.a: The teacher waited ten extra seconds instead of moving on, which let Harsha finish thinking and share the key idea.

qa.q: How might Avni see the extra ten seconds?
qa.a: Avni, whose hand went up first, might feel impatient, but also gets to hear a deeper idea she might not have reached.

grounding: It illustrates a child's silence, looking away and chin-tapping as signs of thinking, and a teacher's extra wait letting the child finish.

passage:
"Papa, can we just go home?" Yogesh stood at the clinic door, gripping the frame.
Yash crouched down. "You're not sure about the check-up?"
"What will she do to me?"
"Let's preview it. The doctor will look in your ears with a little torch, listen to your chest with a cold metal circle, and ask you some questions. Want to practise?"
Yogesh nodded. Yash made a torch with his fingers. "Say aah."
"Aaah."
"Now the cold circle." He pressed a finger on Yogesh's shirt. Yogesh giggled.
"Will you stay?"
"The whole time. I'll sit right where you can see me."
Yogesh let go of the frame, one finger at a time. "Okay. But you say aah first."

qa.q: Where was Yogesh standing when he asked to go home?
qa.a: At the clinic door, gripping the frame.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling as he gripped the door frame?
qa.a: He felt apprehensive and unsure about what the doctor would do, so he held back.

qa.q: Which steps helped Yogesh let go of the frame?
qa.a: A preview of what would happen, a playful practice, and Yash's promise to sit where Yogesh could see him.

qa.q: How might Yash see his son's hanging back?
qa.a: Yash seems to see a cautious pause rather than naughtiness, so he crouches, asks and prepares Yogesh instead of pulling him in.

grounding: It shows a child hanging back before a doctor visit and the apprehension easing with a preview, practice and a supportive parent.

passage:
"It was right here. I put the key on this bench before PT. Aman, if Mummy finds out I lost the house key again..."
"Breathe. Checked your blazer?"
"Twice!"
Amandeep crawled under the bench. "Bottle bag?"
"Checked!" Leela's voice was high and thin.
"Water tank?"
"Why would it be at the..."
"Found it!" Amandeep held up the key; it had been hanging on the tap by its red string.
Leela let out a huge breath and sank onto the bench, arms flopping. Then she started laughing and couldn't stop.
"You look like you've run a marathon," said Amandeep.
"I feel like I've been awake for a week. Why did I hang it on the tap?"
"Because you were thirsty, genius."

qa.q: Where was the key found?
qa.a: Hanging on the tap by its red string.

qa.q: What was Leela feeling when her voice went high and thin?
qa.a: She felt anxious and panicky, worried about Mummy finding out she had lost the house key again.

qa.q: What helped the search work?
qa.a: Amandeep stayed calm, told Leela to breathe, and checked places one by one, including an unlikely one 👍

qa.q: How might Amandeep read Leela's slump on the bench?
qa.a: Amandeep jokes that she looks as if she has run a marathon, reading the drop as tiredness, though it is really relief after the tension.

grounding: It illustrates a child's big exhale, slump and laughter when a lost key turns up, with the drop in the body looking like tiredness.

passage: I'm Lavanya, and the night before my first big science test last term, I couldn't settle. What if I forgot the parts of a flower? What if the paper had questions we never did? My stomach twisted, and I got up three times for water. Alka didi was studying at the other desk. She didn't say, "Don't worry." She said, "Tell me all the what-ifs." I told her every one, and she wrote them down. Then we made a small plan: read my flower notes once, write a list of three things I knew for sure, and sleep by ten. In the morning my stomach still fluttered, but the list was in my pocket, and I read it before the paper started.

qa.q: Where was Lavanya's list on the morning of the test?
qa.a: In Lavanya's pocket.

qa.q: What was Lavanya worried about the night before the test?
qa.a: Lavanya felt anxious about forgetting the flower parts or meeting unfamiliar questions, and the worry showed as a twisting stomach.

qa.q: Why did Alka didi's approach work better than "Don't worry"?
qa.a: She listened to every what-if, wrote them down and turned them into a simple plan, which gave the worry somewhere to go.

qa.q: What might Alka didi have noticed that night?
qa.a: She likely noticed Lavanya getting up for water again and again and read it as worry, so she paused her own study to listen.

grounding: It shows a child's pre-test worry appearing as what-if questions and a twisting stomach, eased by an older sibling listening and making a simple plan.
